newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakh govt annuls uranium deal with Canadian firm.
newsitem.headline: Kazakh govt annuls uranium deal with Canadian firm.

text.p: Kazakhstan has cancelled a deal with Canada's World Wide Minerals Ltd to manage a uranium company, but the company has threatened to appeal to international arbitration to have the contract reinstated.

"The government saw no prospects for further cooperation with (this) company," Birzhan Madiyev, a department head at the finance ministry's state property department, told a news conference on Tuesday.
In October last year the ex-Soviet state and the Toronto-based firm signed a deal for management of the state-run Tselinny uranium company in northern Kazakhstan's.
Madiyev said that under the contract the Canadian firm had to pay off within 15 months pension and salary arrears of $4.5 million which the combine inherited from its former management.
But he said this condition was not being fulfilled, because the company had not made payments for the last few months. "This is the main reason for breaking the contract," he added.

World Wide officials said their company -- represented at Tselinny by its subsidiary KazUran Corporation -- has been paying all wages on time and has managed to stabilise uranium output in northern Kazakhstan.

They also said the unilateral cancellation of the deal by the Kazakh side was against one of the contract's clauses, which stipulates that the contract can be annulled only after one side notifies another about it 90 days before such action.
But the government notified the Canadian firm about cancelling the contract on July 28, issuing a relevant order on August 2, the company said.

"Now there are two variants -- either both sides...restore the status quo...or we appeal to international arbitration," Igor Anchevsky, Vice President of World Wide Minerals, told the same news conference. "We are confident we will win."
Madiyev looked unruffled. "We are getting ready for possible legal consequences," he said, but did not elaborate.
Anchevsky said the firm had already invested some $20 million in the combine, which employs over 8,000 workers.
Yuri Mover, KazUran Vice President, said that under the contract the Canadian firm had to invest a total of $150 million in Tselinny within five years.
Mover said until now KazUran had managed to produce 50 tonnes of uranium but could not export it, because the government had not issued the necessary export licence.

"None of this has been sold, because if there is no licence, nothing can be exported," he said, adding that the absence of the licence was casting uncertainty over a deal to supply uranium to a company in the United States.
Madiyev said the issue of the licence had to be decided by some "competent bodies", but gave no further information.
Kazakhstan has a quarter of the world's uranium ore, but output has fallen to 1,240 tonnes from 3,200 tonnes a year in Soviet times.
